source_text:
Ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς ὁ τὴν
ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων αὐθαιρέτως προιέμενος. Ὥσπερ οὖν ἐν μορφῇ θεοῦ ὑπάρχων ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσα μορφὴν δούλου λαβὼν μηδενὸς ἀναγκά σαντος, οὕτω καὶ ἑκοντὶ τὸν θάνατον ὑπομένω οὐ βίᾳ κρατούμε νος, ἀλλ' αὐθαιρέτως ἐπὶ τὸ πάθος ἐρχόμενος. ∆ιὰ τί δὲ ἔπαθες, δέσποτα; ∆ιὰ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίαν, φησίν. Καὶ λέγω τὸν τρόπον. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ ἀποφάσει θανάτου τὸ γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων ὑπεβλήθη διὰ τὸν ἐκ παρθενικῆς γῆς πλασθέντα Ἀδάμ, ἐγὼ δὲ ἤμην ὁ τὴν ἀπόφασιν τοῦ θανάτου ἐκβαλών, ἀδύνατον δὲ ἦν τῆς τιμωρίας ἀνεθῆναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον, εἰ μὴ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀνεκαλεσάμην ἀπόφασιν, διὰ τοῦτο ἐκ παρθενικῆς γαστρὸς καθ' ὁμοιότητα τοῦ Ἀδὰμ ἀνθρώπου μορφὴν λαβὼν ὑπομένω θάνατον, ἵνα καὶ ὡς θεὸς λύσω τὴν ἀπόφασιν καὶ ὡς ἄνθρωπος ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καταδέξωμαι τὸν θάνατον. Τοῦτο δὲ ποιῶ, ἵνα μὴ αὐθεντίᾳ, ἀλλὰ συμπαθείᾳ τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐλευθερώσω. Εἰ γὰρ ἀνθρώπου ἁμαρτήσαντος θεὸς ἦν ὁ κατορθώσας, οὐ μέγα ἦν τὸ κατορθούμενον. Νῦν δὲ διὰ τοῦτο ἄνθρωπος γέγονα καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ καταλύσαντος τὸν νόμον τὸν νόμον ἐπλήρωσα, ἵνα τῇ οἰκειότητι τοῦ κατορθώσαντος ἐνα βρύνηται τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ γένος. Ὅθεν καὶ νῦν εἰς πρόσωπον τοῦ Ἀδὰμ δέχομαι τὴν ἀπόφασιν τοῦ θανάτου, ἵνα ἐκεῖνος δι' ἐμοῦ λάβῃ τὴν χάριν τῆς ἀναστάσεως. Πταίσας ὁ Ἀδὰμ συνεισήνεγκε τὸν θάνατον, κατορθώσας ἐγὼ ἀντεισήγαγον τὴν ἀνάστασιν. Καὶ ἐπειδὴ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ Ἀδὰμ μέχρι Μωϋσέως, ἐβασί λευσεν δὲ ἐκ τοῦ τὸ σῶμα ὑποχείριον ἔχειν τὸ συνεργὸν τῆς ἁμαρτίας, διὰ τοῦτο ἀνέλαβον τὸ αὐτὸ σῶμα τὸ δοκοῦν ὄργανον εἶναι τῆς ἁμαρτίας, <ἵνα> καταργήσας τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἐλεύθερον ἁμαρτίας ἀποδείξω τὸν ἄνθρωπον. Ἄλλως δὲ ἐπειδὴ ζωὴν κακὴν ἔζων οἱ ἄνθρωποι συμπεπλεγμένοι τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ὡς εἶναι αὐτῶν τὴν ζωὴν θανάτου χείρονα, διὰ τοῦτο τὸν ἀγαθὸν θάνατον τῆς κακῆς ζωῆς προκρίνας ὑπομένω θάνατον, ἵνα οἱ τῷ καλῷ θανάτῳ κοινωνήσαντες τῆς ἀληθοῦς ζωῆς ἀπολαύσωσιν· ἀπολαύσωσιν δὲ διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος· Ὅσοι γὰρ βαπτίζονται, εἰς τὸν θάνατόν μου βαπτίζονται, ἵνα ὥσπερ ἠγέρθην ἐγὼ ἐκ νεκρῶν, οὕτως καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐν καινότητι ζωῆς περιπατήσωσιν. Καὶ μηδεὶς ἀμφιβάλλων λεγέτω ὅτι τὸ σκότος οὐκ ἐργάζεται φῶς οὔτε τὸ μέλαν ἀποτελεῖ λευκότητα, πῶς ὁ θάνατος ἐγέννη σεν ζωήν; Ὅτι γὰρ ὑπὲρ φύσιν τὸ πρᾶγμα, δῆλον. Ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἐμοῦ μὴ ζήτει φύσεως τάξιν. Ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι ὁ δεσπότης τῆς φύσεως, ὁ ποτὲ μὲν τὴν φύσιν κατὰ φύσιν φέρεσθαι συγχωρῶν, ποτὲ δὲ αὐτὴν ὑπὲρ φύσιν ἡνιοχῶν. Ὅταν γάρ τι ἐξαίσιον οἰκονομῆσαι θέλω, τότε καὶ ἡ φύσις τὴν ἑαυτῆς ἀρνησαμένη τάξιν ἐκεῖνα πράττει, ἅπερ ἂν τὸ ἐμὸν παρακελεύηται νεῦμα. Καὶ τοῦτο δῆλον ἐκ τῆς ὁρωμένης διακοσμήσεως, οἷόν τι λέγω· ὁ ἥλιος καὶ ἡ σελήνη πῦρ εἰσιν κατὰ φύσιν, ὕδωρ δὲ τὸ κρυσταλλωθὲν στερέω μα, ὃ δὴ οὐρανὸν ἐκάλεσα· εἰ φύσεως οὖν δρόμον ἐπιζητεῖς, πῶς τὸ πῦρ ὑπὸ 3 τοῦ ὕδατος φυλάττεται ἢ τὸ κρυσταλλωθὲν στερέωμα πῶς ὑπὸ τῆς θέρμης τοῦ πυρὸς οὐ διαλύεται καὶ διαρρεῖ; Καὶ ἵνα σου τὴν ψυχὴν μὴ περὶ τὴν ὁρωμένην διακόσμησιν ἀσχολήσω, ἐπ' αὐτήν σε τὴν οἰκονομίαν χειραγωγήσας πείθω ὡς οὐ χρὴ ἐπὶ ταῖς παραδόξοις θαυματουργίαις φύσεως ἐπιζητεῖν δρόμον. Ἀναλόγισαι γὰρ ὅτι θεὸς ὢν ἀνθρώπινον ὑπεδύην σῶμα. Τοῦτο δὲ πρῶτον παρὰ φύσιν. Ἐπεὶ πῶς τὸ τριχῇ διάστατον σῶμα τὸ ἀνθρώπινον τὸν ἀχώρητον, τὸν ἀμέτρητον, τὸν πανταχοῦ ὄντα, τὸν πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην περιγράφοντα, τὸν μετροῦντα τὸν οὐρανὸν σπιθαμῇ καὶ τὴν γῆν δρακὶ καὶ τὴν θάλατταν κοτύλῃ χωρῆσαι ἠδύνατο, εἰπέ. Ὅτι γὰρ ἐχώρησεν δῆλον, ἐπειδὴ καὶ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τῆς θεότητος ἐνῴκησεν ἐν τῇ σαρκὶ σωματικῶς. Τὸ δὲ πῶς ἐγὼ μὲν οἶδα, φησίν. Οἶδα γὰρ ἃ οἰκονομῶ, σὺ δὲ ἀκοῦσαι οὐ δύνῃ· ὑπερβαίνει γὰρ ἀκοὴν θνητὴν ἡ τῶν ἀπορρήτων εἴδησις οὕτως, ὅτι κἂν ποτὲ διὰ πλῆθος οἰκτιρμῶν ἑρμηνεῦσαί τι θέλω, οὕτως ἑρμηνεύω, οὐχ ὡς ἡ φύσις ἔχει, ἀλλ' ὡς σὺ μαθεῖν δύνῃ· διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ καὶ τῶν δοκήσει σοφῶν τὸν τῦφον καταστέλλων ἔλεγον· Ὁ δοκῶν εἰδέναι τι, οὐδέπω οὐδὲν ἔγνωκεν, καθὼς δεῖ γνῶναι. Ἐπεὶ ὅτι λόγος ὢν σὰρξ γέγονα, ἤκουσας, τὸ δὲ πῶς ἀγνοεῖς. Πῶς γὰρ ἤμην ἐν τῇ σαρκί, ὡς σῶμα ἐν σώματι ἢ ὡς ψυχὴ ἐν σώματι; Οὐκοῦν συνέπαθον τῷ παθητῷ σώματι, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔπαθον. Θεοῦ γὰρ φύσις οὐ περιπίπτει πάθει. Ὥσπερ οὖν σὰρξ γέγονα οὐκ ἐκπεσὼν τοῦ εἶναι θεός, οὕτως καὶ πάθος ὑπέμεινα οὐ περιπεσὼν πάθει. Ἐγεννήθην δι' οἰκονομίαν, ἀπέθα νον διὰ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων σωτηρίαν· μᾶλλον δὲ διὰ τοῦτο ἀπέθανον, ἐπειδὴ ἐγεννήθην.
thought_title: Christ explains why he willingly undergoes death
orientation: Christ is speaking in the first person, explaining to the heretics that his fear and death are a deliberate plan of salvation, not weakness.
pass_a_gloss: For I am the good shepherd, the one who lays down his own soul for the sheep of his own free will. Just as, then, being in the form of God, I emptied myself, taking the form of a slave, no one having compelled me, so also willingly I endure death, not being overpowered by force, but of my own free will coming to the passion. But why did you suffer, Master? For the salvation of human beings, he says. And I tell the manner. For since by a sentence of death the race of human beings was subjected through Adam, who was formed from virgin earth, and I was the one who had issued the sentence of death, and it was impossible for the human being to be released from the punishment unless I myself recalled my own sentence, for this reason, taking the form of a human being from a virgin womb according to the likeness of Adam, I endure death, so that both as God I may dissolve the sentence and as a human being I may accept death on behalf of human beings. And this I do, so that not by authority but by compassion I may set the human being free. For if, when a human being had sinned, it was God who had set things right, the thing set right was not great. But now for this reason I have become a human being and on behalf of the one who broke the law I have fulfilled the law, so that by the kinship of the one who set things right the race of human beings may glory. For which reason even now in the person of Adam I receive the sentence of death, so that that one through me may receive the grace of the resurrection. Adam, having stumbled, brought in death together with himself; I, having set things right, brought in resurrection in return. And since death reigned from Adam until Moses, and it reigned by having the body as a subject, the body being the co-worker of sin, for this reason I took up the same body that seemed to be the instrument of sin, so that, having abolished sin, I may show the human being free from sin. And otherwise, since human beings were living an evil life, entangled with sin, so that their life was worse than death, for this reason, having preferred the good death to the evil life, I endure death, so that those who have shared in the good death may enjoy the true life; and they may enjoy it through baptism. For as many as are baptized, into my death they are baptized, so that just as I was raised from the dead, so also they may walk in newness of life. And let no one, doubting, say that darkness does not produce light nor does black produce whiteness, how did death beget life? For that the matter is beyond nature is clear. But in my case do not seek the order of nature. For I am the master of nature, the one who sometimes allows nature to be borne according to nature, and sometimes drives it beyond nature. For whenever I wish to arrange something extraordinary, then nature also, having denied its own order, does those things which my nod commands. And this is clear from the visible ordering of the world, such as I mean: the sun and the moon are fire by nature, and the water that has been frozen is a firmament, which indeed I called heaven. If, then, you seek the course of nature, how is the fire guarded by the water, or how is the frozen firmament not dissolved and does not flow away by the heat of the fire? And so that I may not occupy your soul with the visible ordering of the world, having led you by the hand to the plan of salvation itself, I persuade you that it is not necessary to seek the course of nature in paradoxical wonders. For consider that, being God, I put on a human body. And this is first beyond nature. For how was the three-dimensionally extended human body able to contain the uncontainable one, the immeasurable one, the one who is everywhere, the one who circumscribes the whole inhabited world, the one who measures the heaven with a span and the earth with a handful and the sea with a cup, tell me. For that it did contain him is clear, since also all the fullness of the divinity dwelt in the flesh bodily. But the how, I know, he says. For I know what I arrange, but you are not able to hear; for the knowledge of ineffable things surpasses mortal hearing so much that even if ever through the abundance of mercies I wish to interpret something, I interpret it thus, not as nature has it, but as you are able to learn. For this reason also, suppressing the vanity of those who seem wise, I was saying: The one who seems to know something, has not yet known anything, as it is necessary to know. Since, then, that being Word I became flesh, you have heard, but the how you do not know. For how was I in the flesh, as a body in a body or as a soul in a body? Therefore I suffered together with the passible body, but I did not suffer. For the nature of God does not fall into passion. Just as, then, I became flesh without falling out of being God, so also I endured passion without falling into passion. I was born through the plan of salvation, I died for the salvation of human beings; rather, for this reason I died, because I was born.

choices.why: The adverb emphasizes Christ's voluntary self-giving, central to the argument against the heretics' charge of fear.
The term denotes a judicial decree or condemnation, fitting the legal metaphor of death's reign and Christ's recall of his own decree.
The verb implies successful accomplishment of what is right, contrasting Adam's stumble with Christ's corrective act.
The adjective means under one's hand or power, conveying death's dominion over the body as sin's instrument.
The charioteer metaphor conveys Christ's sovereign control over nature, steering it beyond its own order.
The verb implies gentle, personal guidance, fitting Christ's pastoral tone in leading the hearer to the plan of salvation.

pass_b_english: For I am the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep of his own free will (John 10:11). Just as, though I existed in the form of God, I emptied myself and took the form of a servant with no one forcing me (Philippians 2:6-7), so also I endure death willingly—not overpowered by force, but coming to the passion of my own free will. “Why then did you suffer, Master?” “For the salvation of human beings,” he says. And I will tell you the manner of it. Since the human race was made subject to the sentence of death through Adam, who was formed from virgin earth, and since I was the one who had cast out the sentence of death, it was impossible for the human being to be released from the punishment unless I myself recalled my own sentence. For this reason I took human form from a virgin womb, in the likeness of Adam, and I endure death, so that as God I may dissolve the sentence, and as a human being I may accept death on behalf of human beings. I do this so that I may set humanity free not by authority but by compassion. For if a human being had sinned and God had set things right, the achievement would not have been great. But as it is, for this reason I became a human being, and on behalf of the one who broke the law I fulfilled the law, so that the human race might glory in the kinship of the one who set things right. Therefore even now I receive the sentence of death on behalf of Adam, so that through me he may receive the grace of the resurrection. Adam stumbled and brought death in with him; I set things right and brought the resurrection in against it. And since death reigned from Adam until Moses (Romans 5:14)—and it reigned by holding the body subject as the co-worker of sin—for this reason I took up that same body which seemed to be the instrument of sin, so that by abolishing sin I might show the human being free from sin. And in another way: since human beings were living an evil life, entangled with sin, so that their life was worse than death, for this reason I chose the good death over the evil life and endure death, so that those who share in the good death may enjoy the true life. And they enjoy it through baptism. For all who are baptized are baptized into my death, so that just as I was raised from the dead, so also they may walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3-4). And let no one doubt and say, “Darkness does not produce light, nor does black produce whiteness—how then did death give birth to life?” That the matter is beyond nature is clear. But in my case do not look for the order of nature. For I am the master of nature, sometimes allowing nature to run according to nature, and sometimes driving it beyond nature. For whenever I wish to accomplish something extraordinary, then nature denies its own order and does whatever my command directs. And this is clear from the visible order of creation—I mean something like this: the sun and the moon are fire by nature, and the frozen water is a firmament, which I called heaven. If you look for the course of nature, how is the fire guarded by the water, or how is the frozen firmament not dissolved and melted by the heat of the fire? And so that I may not occupy your soul with the visible order of creation, I will lead you by the hand to the plan of salvation itself and persuade you that in paradoxical wonders one must not look for the course of nature. Consider that though I was God, I put on a human body. This is first of all beyond nature. For tell me, how could the human body, extended in three dimensions, contain the one who cannot be contained, the one without measure, the one who is everywhere, the one who circumscribes the whole world, the one who measures the heaven with a span and the earth with a handful and the sea with a cup (Isaiah 40:12)? That it did contain him is clear, since all the fullness of divinity dwelt in the flesh bodily (Colossians 2:9). But how—I know, he says. For I know what I arrange in my plan of salvation, but you cannot hear it. For the knowledge of ineffable things surpasses mortal hearing, so much so that even when I wish to explain something because of the abundance of my mercies, I explain it not as nature has it, but as you are able to learn. For this reason, putting down the pride of those who seem wise, I said: “The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2). For you have heard that though I was the Word, I became flesh, but how—you do not know. How was I in the flesh—as a body in a body, or as a soul in a body? I shared in the suffering of the passible body, then, but I did not suffer. For the nature of God does not fall into passion. Just as I became flesh without ceasing to be God, so also I endured the passion without falling into passion. I was born for the plan of salvation; I died for the salvation of human beings. Rather, I died for this reason: because I was born.

problems.quote: I receive the sentence of death in the person of Adam
problems.source_quote: νῦν εἰς πρόσωπον τοῦ Ἀδὰμ δέχομαι τὴν ἀπόφασιν τοῦ θανάτου
problems.why: εἰς πρόσωπον means 'on behalf of' or 'for the sake of,' not 'in the person of.' Christ dies as Adam's substitute/representative, not 'in his person.'
problems.fix: I receive the sentence of death on behalf of Adam

problems.quote: I became a human being for this reason, and I fulfilled the law on behalf of the one who broke the law
problems.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἄνθρωπος γέγονα καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ καταλύσαντος τὸν νόμον τὸν νόμον ἐπλήρωσα
problems.why: The Greek καὶ connects two parallel clauses: 'I became human AND I fulfilled the law.' The English 'for this reason... and' weakens the explicit parallelism of the two saving acts.
problems.fix: for this reason I became a human being, and on behalf of the one who broke the law I fulfilled the law

problems.quote: the one who had issued the sentence of death
problems.why: ἐκβαλών means 'cast out/removed' the sentence, not 'issued' it. Christ removes death's sentence, he doesn't issue it.
problems.fix: the one who had cast out the sentence of death
problems.ruling: ἐκβαλών means 'casting out/away', not 'issuing'; Christ removes death's sentence, opposite meaning.

problems.quote: it reigned by holding the body subject as the instrument of sin
problems.source_quote: ἐβασίλευσεν δὲ ἐκ τοῦ τὸ σῶμα ὑποχείριον ἔχειν τὸ συνεργὸν τῆς ἁμαρτίας
problems.why: Source: death reigned by holding the body subject as sin's co-worker. English 'as the instrument of sin' loses συνεργόν (co-worker/fellow-worker).
problems.fix: it reigned by holding the body subject as the co-worker of sin
problems.ruling: συνεργόν means 'co-worker', not 'instrument'; active partner in sin is lost.

edits.old: I receive the sentence of death in the person of Adam
edits.new: I receive the sentence of death on behalf of Adam

edits.old: I became a human being for this reason, and I fulfilled the law on behalf of the one who broke the law
edits.new: for this reason I became a human being, and on behalf of the one who broke the law I fulfilled the law

edits.old: the one who had issued the sentence of death
edits.new: the one who had cast out the sentence of death

edits.old: it reigned by holding the body subject as the instrument of sin
edits.new: it reigned by holding the body subject as the co-worker of sin

The Greek καὶ connects two parallel clauses; restored the parallelism.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς ὁ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων αὐθαιρέτως προιέμενος
last_rejected.why: The source quotes John 10:11 but with the addition of αὐθαιρέτως (of his own free will), which is not in the biblical text. The English should note this adaptation or not cite the verse as exact.
last_rejected.fix: For I am the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep of his own free will (cf. John 10:11).
last_rejected.ruling: Citation is correct; αὐθαιρέτως is author's gloss, not translator error.

last_rejected.quote: the frozen water is a firmament, which I called heaven
last_rejected.source_quote: ὕδωρ δὲ τὸ κρυσταλλωθὲν στερέωμα, ὃ δὴ οὐρανὸν ἐκάλεσα
last_rejected.why: The Greek says the crystallized/frozen solid (στερέωμα) is what 'I called heaven,' not that the frozen water is a firmament which I called heaven. The syntax is ὕδωρ δὲ τὸ κρυσταλλωθὲν [is] στερέωμα, ὃ δὴ οὐρανὸν ἐκάλεσα.
last_rejected.fix: and the crystallized water is a firmament, which I called heaven
last_rejected.ruling: ὕδωρ τὸ κρυσταλλωθὲν στερέωμα = 'frozen water [is] firmament'; English captures this correctly.

last_rejected.quote: I shared in the suffering of the passible body, then, but I did not suffer
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐκοῦν συνέπαθον τῷ παθητῷ σώματι, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔπαθον
last_rejected.why: συνέπαθον means 'I suffered with' or 'I had compassion with,' not merely 'shared in the suffering.' The English weakens the paradox of Christ's co-suffering with the body while remaining impassible in his divine nature.
last_rejected.fix: I suffered with the passible body, then, but I did not suffer
last_rejected.ruling: συνέπαθον with dative = 'shared in suffering'; English is within normal range, not a major error.
